_about.what: Verification status of each intervention in the county-bundle catalog (D.catalog). The page shows a dollar or $-per-$1 figure only for verified and partially_verified items; unverified items are listed by name only.

status.verified: effect size and cost both confirmed against a source fetched in the audit
status.partially_verified: one side confirmed (or, for items with no dollar effect, the cost cites a named public document that was not re-fetched)
status.unverified: neither confirmed, source not found, not reproducible, or labelled an unchecked AI research pass in the catalog

effect.checked: the effect size used was found in the cited source's text
effect.unchecked: the study exists or is named, but the number used was not confirmed (or the item estimates no dollar effect)
effect.misapplied: the number is real but applied outside the conditions the study measured
effect.not_found: the cited study or its data could not be found

cost.checked: the unit cost was found in a fetched document
cost.unchecked: the cost cites a document that was not re-fetched, or has no source
cost.contradicted: the cost used differs materially from the document it cites

street_trees.evidence: City Pretty local hedonic (3,386 Westside sales): no regression code or sales data in repo or git history; irreproducible. Shipped to 637 non-LA counties as "local sales estimate".
street_trees.notes: Unverified: the catalog's grade-A effect comes from a 'City Pretty local hedonic' regression (3,386 Westside sales, 2022-24) whose code and sales data are not in the repository or its git history, so it cannot be reproduced. Confirmed street-tree studies exist in research/effects.csv (Donovan & Butry 2010; Sander, Polasky & Haight 2010) but the model does not use them yet. The same 0.24% was shipped to 637 non-LA counties labelled 'local sales estimate'. Cost cites a named public document that was not re-fetched (most LA agency sites return 403 from the audit machine). | 2026-11-16 re-check: Donovan & Butry 2010 measured the bundle of existing street trees fronting a house (+3.0% of median price), not newly planted trees within 50 m, so it does not confirm the engine's 0.24% per new tree. Round 3 (16 Nov): the closest study of new plantings, Wachter & Wong (2008), What Is a Tree Worth? Green-City Strategies, Signaling and Housing Prices, Real Estate Economics, doi:10.1111/j.1540-6229.2008.00212.x, found: "A 7 to 11% price differential is identified within 4,000 feet of the Fairmount tree plantings. ... Any positive changes brought by the PHS tree plantings were not detected with sufficient statistical power." It is correlational, not a per-tree estimate, and the community block-planting program (the kind City Pretty would recommend) showed no detectable effect, so it does not support a dollar figure.

street_lighting.evidence: Effect, re-derived from two fetched sources: (1) Chalfin, Hansen, Lerner & Parker (2019), NBER Working Paper 25798, doi:10.3386/w25798: "Accounting conservatively for potential spillovers, lighting reduces outdoor nighttime index crimes by approximately 36 percent and reduces overall index crimes by approximately 4 percent in affected communities." (2) Pope & Pope (2012), Crime and property values: Evidence from the 1990s crime drop, Regional Science and Urban Economics, doi:10.1016/j.regsciurbeco.2011.08.008: "The estimated elasticities of property values with respect to crime range from -0.15 to -0.35." Using the low end: 4% fewer index crimes x 0.15 = +0.6% home value.
street_lighting.notes: The bundle used +1.358% (36% x an assumed 32.5% nighttime-outdoor share x an unverified 0.116 elasticity). Chalfin et al. state the share directly: "On NYC's public housing campuses, approximately 11 percent of index crimes occur outdoors and during nighttime hours." and give the overall effect (4%), so +0.6% replaces it. Limits: the trial was on NYC public-housing campuses; Pope & Pope is zip-code level (1990s) and mostly correlational; the engine applies the effect to 30% of the block group's homes (a model choice, not from either study). Cost (~$5,000 per 50-ft lot, LA Bureau of Street Lighting) not re-fetched.

sourced_effect.basis: 4% fewer index crimes (Chalfin et al. 2019, NYC lighting RCT) x the low-end crime elasticity of home values, 0.15 (Pope & Pope 2012).

ev_hub.evidence: Effect: Liang, Qiu, Liu, He & Mauzerall (2023), Nature Sustainability, doi:10.1038/s41893-022-01058-5 (abstract on nature.com fetched 2026-11-16): "The average price premium for houses with EVCSs within 1 km is about 3.3% (or US$17,212) compared with homes without proximate EVCSs." Cost: California Transportation Commission baseline agreement, SBCAG / City of Santa Barbara ZEV Charging Infrastructure project report (Nov 2025), p. 171: "Eight DC Fast Chargers (DCFC) will be installed at this location. ... Total Project Cost $1,777,000 Outputs 8 DC charging ports" (https://catc.ca.gov/-/media/ctc-media/documents/programs/baseline-agreements/2026-01/5-sbcag-ba-sb-us-101.pdf).
ev_hub.notes: 'Liang et al. 2023 (14M California sales) +3.3%' could not be found (the closest Crossref match is an unrelated preprint about EV sales); the 1% used is a self-declared discount of that unfound number. The CARB 8-port site cost is also unverified in the catalog. | Round 4 (16 Nov): Correction to the round-1 audit, which said 'Liang et al. 2023' could not be found: it is Liang et al., Nature Sustainability (2023), and its abstract states the +3.3% within 1 km the catalog cited. The engine used 1.0% and $800,000 for an 8-port site; a public project report budgets $1,777,000, so returns were overstated about 2.2x on cost. Both are replaced by the sourced figures. Remains partly verified: the effect is an association, and the cost is one planned project. Applied only in California: the study's sample is California-only (applies_if.state_fips_in); elsewhere no dollar figure is shown.

sourced_effect.basis: Homes with a public EV charging station within 1 km sold for about 3.3% more (hedonic association, 14 million California sales, 1993-2021; not a causal estimate). Cost: one planned 8-port DC fast site, Santa Barbara, $1,777,000 total project cost (Nov 2025 report; includes design and site work).

citations.cite: Liang, Qiu, Liu, He & Mauzerall (2023), Effects of expanding electric vehicle charging stations in California on the housing market, Nature Sustainability, doi:10.1038/s41893-022-01058-5
citations.quote: The average price premium for houses with EVCSs within 1 km is about 3.3% (or US$17,212) compared with homes without proximate EVCSs.
